why.correct: A cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion. Ganglia appear as small swellings along nerves, and they belong to the PNS.
options: A nucleus is also a cluster of cell bodies, but it lies inside the CNS. This swelling sits outside the spinal cord, in the PNS.
A tract is a bundle of axons inside the CNS, not a swelling on a nerve.
Correct. A swelling on a nerve that holds neuron cell bodies is a ganglion.
Gray matter is CNS tissue. This structure lies outside the brain and spinal cord.

why.correct: The spinal cord runs down from the brain inside the vertebral column. With the brain, it forms the central nervous system.
options: Correct. The long central column running down from the brain is the spinal cord, part of the CNS.
Nerves branch off the spinal cord and run out into the body. The pinned structure is the central column they branch from.
A ganglion is a small swelling on a nerve, not the long central column.
Tracts are bundles of axons inside the CNS, too small to see on a whole-body drawing. The pinned structure is the whole spinal cord.

why.correct: The PNS is everything outside the brain and spinal cord: nerves, ganglia and sensory receptors. The spinal cord and the brain's gray matter are CNS.
options: Yes. Nerves run outside the CNS, so they are PNS.
No. The spinal cord and the brain together make up the CNS.
Yes. A ganglion is a cluster of cell bodies outside the CNS, so it is PNS.
Yes. Sensory receptors sit at the ends of PNS axons, out in the tissues.
No. Gray matter is found in the brain and spinal cord, so it is CNS tissue.

why.correct: The sensory division is also called the afferent division: afferent signals arrive at the CNS, carrying input from sensory receptors.
options: The motor (efferent) division carries signals away from the CNS, out to effectors.
Correct. Sensory, or afferent, axons carry signals in toward the CNS.
The somatic nervous system is part of the motor division. It carries commands out to skeletal muscle.
The parasympathetic division is part of the autonomic motor output, so its signals travel away from the CNS.

why.correct: The signals start at sensory receptors and travel toward the CNS, so they are carried by the sensory (afferent) division. Sensory input comes from internal organs as well as from the skin.
options: The somatic nervous system is motor output to skeletal muscle. These signals are traveling in, not out.
The motor division carries signals away from the CNS. These travel toward the brain.
Correct. Input from sensory receptors, heading to the CNS, travels in the sensory division.
The sympathetic division carries commands out from the CNS. It does not carry sensory input in.

why.correct: The somatic nervous system controls skeletal muscle, the muscle attached to your skeleton. The other effectors belong to the autonomic nervous system.
options: Correct. Somatic motor neurons run to skeletal muscles.
Cardiac muscle and glands are autonomic effectors.
Smooth muscle in vessel walls is controlled by the autonomic nervous system.
This is the full list of autonomic effectors, not somatic ones.

why.correct: Shivering is rapid contraction of skeletal muscles, and skeletal muscle is controlled only by the somatic nervous system. "Voluntary" is a useful rule of thumb for somatic output, but the effector is what defines the division.
options: Shivering is involuntary, but the autonomic nervous system does not reach skeletal muscle. Its effectors are cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands.
Correct. The effector is skeletal muscle, so the commands travel in somatic motor neurons.
The skin's sensory receptors detect the cold, and the sensory division carries that input in. The commands that produce shivering travel out, in the motor division.
The parasympathetic division is autonomic and has no axons to skeletal muscle, so it cannot produce shivering.

why.correct: The autonomic nervous system controls cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands: heart rate, sweat glands and the smooth muscle of the gut. Writing and deliberate blinking use skeletal muscle, so they are somatic.
options: Yes. Heart rate is set by autonomic signals to cardiac muscle.
Yes. Sweat glands are glands, and glands are autonomic effectors.
No. Writing uses skeletal muscles of the hand, controlled by the somatic nervous system.
Yes. The gut wall's smooth muscle is an autonomic effector.
No. The muscles that close your eyes are skeletal muscles, so a deliberate blink is somatic output.

why.correct: Sympathetic (fight-or-flight) activation speeds the heart, makes the palms sweat and slows digestion.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Sympathetic signals to the heart make it beat faster: part of the fight-or-flight pattern.

variables.name: Movement and secretion in the gut
variables.why: Sympathetic signals slow the smooth muscle of the gut and its digestive secretions, so digestion is put on hold.

variables.name: Sweating from the palms
variables.why: Sympathetic axons reach the sweat glands, and sympathetic activation makes them secrete.

why.correct: At rest after a meal, parasympathetic activity dominates: the heart slows and digestion speeds up. Somatic output to the legs drops because you are not moving, a separate change in a separate system.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Parasympathetic signals to the heart slow its beat, and sympathetic drive to the heart falls, so the rate drops.

variables.name: Movement and secretion in the gut
variables.why: Parasympathetic signals stimulate the gut's smooth muscle and digestive glands: rest-and-digest.

variables.name: Commands to skeletal muscles of the legs
variables.why: You are lying still, so somatic motor output to the leg muscles falls. This change is somatic, not autonomic: the autonomic nervous system does not control skeletal muscle.

why.correct: Every nervous system task runs sensory input, then integration, then motor output. The signal goes in through the sensory division, is processed in the CNS, and goes out through the motor division to the effectors.
options: Sensation comes first: sensory receptors detect the change.
The sensory division carries the input to the CNS.
Integration happens in the CNS.
The motor division carries the command out.
The effectors, here skeletal muscles, respond.

why.correct: Between detecting a change and responding to it, the CNS integrates: it combines the input with other information and determines a response.
options: Correct. Integration is the processing step between input and output.
The afferent division carries the sensory input. It is part of the first step, not a separate job between input and output.
Sensation is another word for the first step, sensory input, so it cannot fill the middle.
The effector is what responds to motor output. It comes at the end, not in the middle.

why.correct: Commands going out from the CNS to muscles travel in efferent (motor) axons, not afferent ones. Afferent axons only carry signals toward the CNS.
options: Correct step. Sensory receptors in the skin start the signals.
Correct step. Afferent axons carry input toward the CNS.
Correct step. Integration happens where neurons connect, in gray matter.
This is the wrong step. Signals leaving the CNS travel in efferent axons of the motor division.
Correct step. Skeletal muscles are the effectors that respond.

why.correct: Inside the CNS, a bundle of axons is a tract. The same kind of bundle outside the CNS is a nerve.
options: A nerve is a bundle of axons in the PNS, not the CNS.
A ganglion is a cluster of cell bodies in the PNS.
A nucleus is a cluster of cell bodies in the CNS, not a bundle of axons.
Correct. A CNS bundle of axons is a tract.

why.correct: A cluster of neuron cell bodies inside the CNS, forming an island of gray matter with a shared job, is a nucleus.
options: A ganglion is a cluster of cell bodies too, but it lies in the PNS. This one is inside the brain.
Correct. A CNS cluster of cell bodies with one job is a nucleus.
A tract is a bundle of axons, which forms white matter, not gray matter.
A nerve is a bundle of axons outside the CNS.

why.correct: White matter is mostly bundles of axons, and many are wrapped in layers of fatty glial membrane. That fat reflects light and looks white.
options: White matter does have fewer capillaries than gray matter, but blood supply is not what sets its color. The fat around its axons is.
Cell bodies are concentrated in gray matter, not white matter.
The CNS has very little collagen-rich connective tissue inside it. White matter is axons and glial cells.
Correct. The fatty wrapping around the axons gives white matter its color.

why.correct: In the spinal cord, gray matter forms a butterfly-shaped core and white matter surrounds it. This is the reverse of most of the brain, where gray matter forms the outer layer.
options: A thin outer layer of gray matter is the pattern in most of the brain, not the spinal cord.
Correct. The spinal cord has gray matter inside and white matter outside.
Gray and white matter are separate regions, not mixed evenly.
Ganglia are PNS structures. The spinal cord has its own gray matter inside it.

why.correct: CNS and PNS divide the system by location; somatic and autonomic divide it by function. Both the somatic and the autonomic systems start with neurons in the CNS and send their commands out through PNS nerves.
options: The neurons that control autonomic output, for example those that decide to speed the heart, sit in the brain and spinal cord. Only part of the autonomic system lies in the PNS.
This mixes two separate ways of dividing the system. Both voluntary and involuntary commands start in the CNS and travel out through the PNS.
Correct. Each functional system has CNS neurons that issue commands and PNS axons that carry them.
Many nerves carry somatic motor, autonomic and sensory axons together. That is why a cut at the wrist can cause numbness, weakness and loss of sweating at once.

why.correct: Each finding points to a different kind of axon. Numbness means sensory axons were cut; weak finger muscles mean somatic motor axons to skeletal muscle were cut; dry skin means autonomic axons to the sweat glands were cut. One nerve carried all three.
options: Sensory loss explains the numbness, but not the weak finger muscles or the dry skin.
This explains the numbness and weakness, but sweat glands are autonomic effectors, so losing sweating means autonomic axons were cut too.
Correct. Numbness, weakness and loss of sweating each come from a different kind of axon in the same nerve.
Autonomic loss explains the dry skin, but autonomic axons do not reach skeletal muscle or carry touch.

why.correct: The parasympathetic division is the rest-and-digest branch of the autonomic nervous system: it slows the heart and stimulates the gut.
options: Correct. That is the rest-and-digest pattern.
That is the sympathetic, fight-or-flight pattern.
Skeletal muscle is controlled by the somatic nervous system at all times, not by any autonomic division.
Input from the organs travels in the sensory division. The parasympathetic division is motor output.

why.correct: In the PNS the axon runs in a nerve, and its cell body sits in a ganglion beside the spinal cord. Once inside the CNS the same axon runs on in a tract. Only the name of the bundle changes at the CNS border.
options: A tract is inside the CNS, so it cannot come first on the way from the fingertip.
The axon leaves the fingertip in a nerve, not a ganglion, and inside the CNS it travels in a tract, not a nucleus.
A ganglion lies in the PNS, outside the spinal cord, so it cannot come after the tract.
Correct. Nerve and ganglion in the PNS, then tract in the CNS.

why.correct: The star-shaped cell with many branching processes reaching out to the neurons is an astrocyte.
options: Oligodendrocytes have a few arms that end in myelin wraps around axons, not many fine star-like processes.
Microglial cells are small, with short, fine, bristly processes. This cell is large and star-shaped.
Correct. Its star shape gives the astrocyte its name (astr- = star).
Ependymal cells form a single layer lining a fluid-filled space. This cell sits among the neurons.

why.correct: The row of cube-shaped cells lining a fluid-filled space in the CNS is ependymal cells.
options: Correct. Ependymal cells line the fluid-filled cavities of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord.
Satellite cells cover neuron cell bodies in PNS ganglia. They do not line a fluid-filled space in the CNS.
Astrocyte end-feet wrap capillaries. They are the ends of star-shaped cells, not a lining layer of cells.
Schwann cells wrap axons in the PNS. They are not found lining spaces in the CNS.

why.correct: The small cell with fine, bristly processes is a microglial cell, one of the resident immune cells of the CNS.
options: Astrocytes are much larger, with long star-like processes.
Oligodendrocytes wrap axon segments in myelin. This small cell wraps nothing.
Ependymal cells sit side by side in a lining layer.
Correct. Microglia are the small glia (micro- = small) that patrol the CNS and engulf debris.

why.correct: Flattened glial cells covering the cell body of a neuron in a PNS ganglion are satellite cells.
options: Schwann cells line up along the axon, not over the cell body.
Correct. Satellite cells cover the somas of neurons in ganglia.
Astrocytes do a similar job around neurons, but they are CNS cells. A ganglion is in the PNS.
Microglia are small immune cells of the CNS. They do not form a covering over neurons in PNS ganglia.

why.correct: One process leaves each end of the cell body, one dendrite and one axon, so this is a bipolar neuron.
options: A multipolar neuron has three or more processes. This one has two.
A unipolar neuron has a single process that splits in two. Here two separate processes leave opposite ends of the cell body.
Correct. Two processes, at opposite ends of the soma, make a bipolar neuron.
Interneuron is a functional class, not a shape. The question asks for the shape shown.

why.correct: The short bare gap between two segments of myelin is a node of Ranvier.
options: Correct. Nodes of Ranvier are the gaps between myelin segments, where the axon's membrane is bare.
The axon hillock is where the axon leaves the soma, not a gap between myelin segments.
An axon collateral is a side branch of the axon.
The initial segment is the first stretch of axon after the hillock, before the myelin starts.

why.correct: The initial segment has the densest voltage-gated sodium channels, so it reaches threshold before any other part of the neuron. It is the trigger zone, where action potentials begin.
options: Correct. The initial segment is packed with voltage-gated sodium channels and acts as the trigger zone.
Dendrites have relatively few voltage-gated sodium channels and mostly carry graded potentials.
The soma's membrane has far fewer voltage-gated sodium channels than the initial segment.
Axon terminals release neurotransmitter at the far end of the axon. Action potentials arrive there; they do not start there.

why.correct: The clumps are Nissl bodies, stacks of rough ER with ribosomes. They mark the soma as the neuron's protein factory; the axon relies on proteins shipped out to it by axonal transport.
options: Mitochondria are spread throughout the neuron, including the axon and its terminals. They are not the dark clumps.
Myelin wraps axons, not dendrites, and it is made by glial cells, not stored in the neuron's soma.
Correct. These are Nissl bodies, and their absence from the axon means it depends on the soma for proteins.
Synaptic vesicles are concentrated in the axon terminals, the one place this stain does not show clumps.

why.correct: Graded potentials spread from the dendrites and soma past the hillock to the initial segment, the trigger zone, where the action potential starts and then travels down the axon.
options: Nodes of Ranvier lie along the myelinated axon, after the action potential has already started.
Correct. The initial segment follows the hillock and is where the action potential begins.
Axon collaterals are side branches farther along the axon. They are not the step between the hillock and the axon.
Nissl bodies are rough ER in the soma, not a region the signal passes through.

why.correct: One process that splits in two makes it unipolar (pseudounipolar). Carrying signals from the skin toward the CNS, with its soma in a ganglion, makes it a sensory neuron.
options: A multipolar neuron has many processes leaving its soma. This one has a single stalk that splits in two.
Motor neurons have many dendrites, and their somas sit in the CNS, not in a ganglion.
A bipolar neuron has two separate processes, and interneurons lie entirely inside the CNS.
Correct. This is the typical sensory neuron: unipolar, with its soma in a ganglion.

why.correct: A neuron entirely within the CNS that connects other neurons is an interneuron. Interneurons do the integrating, and they are by far the most numerous neurons.
options: A motor neuron sends its axon out of the CNS to an effector. This one stays inside the spinal cord.
A sensory neuron carries signals in from a sensory receptor, and its soma lies in a ganglion outside the CNS.
Glial cells support neurons but do not pass signals from one neuron to another. This cell is a neuron.
Correct. Interneurons connect other neurons inside the CNS.

why.correct: Multipolar neurons have one axon and many dendrites. They are the most common shape, and include motor neurons and nearly all interneurons, whose somas sit in CNS gray matter.
options: Correct. That is the definition of multipolar.
Correct. Motor neurons have many dendrites and one axon.
Correct. Nearly all interneurons are multipolar.
Incorrect. Multipolar neurons are by far the most common. Bipolar neurons are the rare ones.
Incorrect. Somas in ganglia beside the spinal cord belong to unipolar sensory neurons.

why.correct: Only oligodendrocytes myelinate segments of many different axons, one per arm, and they are found in the CNS, which includes the brain's white matter.
options: A Schwann cell myelinates a single segment of a single axon, and it works in the PNS, not the brain.
Astrocytes regulate the fluid around neurons and wrap capillaries. They do not make myelin.
Satellite cells cover neuron cell bodies in PNS ganglia. They do not make myelin.
Correct. One oligodendrocyte can myelinate segments of dozens of axons.

why.correct: Microglia are the resident immune cells of the CNS. When they detect damage they multiply, move to the spot and clear debris by phagocytosis.
options: Correct. Microglia are the CNS's phagocytes.
Ependymal cells line fluid-filled spaces and help move and make that fluid. They are not phagocytes.
Oligodendrocytes make myelin. They do not engulf debris.
Schwann cells help clear debris after a nerve injury, but they are found in the PNS, not the brain.

why.correct: The far segment degenerates, its debris is cleared, Schwann cells build a guiding tube, the axon regrows along it, and it is remyelinated when it reaches its target.
options: First: cut off from the soma's supply of proteins, the far segment breaks down.
Second: the wreckage is cleared, within a few weeks in the PNS.
Third: the Schwann cells form a column inside the empty connective tissue tube.
Fourth: the regrowing axon follows the tube.
Last: reconnection and new myelin.

why.correct: A forearm nerve is in the PNS, where Schwann cells multiply and form the regeneration tube. Oligodendrocytes are CNS cells and do not form guiding tubes.
options: Correct step. Without proteins from the soma, the far segment breaks down.
Correct step. Schwann cells and macrophages from the blood clear the debris.
This is the wrong step. In the PNS it is Schwann cells, not oligodendrocytes, that form the tube.
Correct step. The sprout follows the Schwann cell tube.
Correct step. Schwann cells remyelinate the regrown axon.

why.correct: 15 cm is 150 mm. At 1 mm per day, 150 mm takes about 150 days, which is about 5 months (150 ÷ 30). In practice it takes a little longer, because the sprouts first have to cross the repair site.
options: 15 days would mean regrowth of 10 mm per day. The distance is 150 mm, not 15 mm.
Correct. 150 mm ÷ 1 mm/day = 150 days, about 5 months.
A year is about 365 days, more than twice as long as 150 mm of regrowth at 1 mm per day.
1.5 days would require regrowth of 100 mm per day, far faster than axons regrow.

why.correct: Regrowing an axon does not require the neuron to divide; it requires a surviving cell body and a path to grow along. In the CNS, oligodendrocytes form no guiding tube, CNS myelin contains proteins that stop growing axons, and astrocytes seal the injury with a scar.
options: Neurons do not divide, but a cut axon regrows from its surviving cell body, as happens in PNS nerves. Division is not the issue.
Most axons in the spinal cord's white matter are myelinated, and myelination is not what allows regrowth.
The question states that the cell bodies survive. Microglia clear debris; they are not the reason the axons fail to regrow.
Correct. The CNS environment, not the neuron's inability to divide, is the main barrier.

why.correct: After a PNS axon is cut, the far segment breaks down, Schwann cells multiply to build a guiding tube, and the cell body steps up protein synthesis to supply regrowth.

variables.name: Intact axon beyond the cut
variables.why: The far segment is cut off from the proteins shipped out from the soma, so it fragments and breaks down within days.

variables.name: Number of Schwann cells at the injured segment
variables.why: Once the myelin debris is cleared, Schwann cells multiply and line up to form the regeneration tube.

variables.name: Protein synthesis in the neuron's cell body
variables.why: The surviving soma swells and ramps up production of the proteins needed to regrow the axon.

why.correct: Myelin is layer on layer of glial plasma membrane, mostly lipid, wrapped around axon segments that are separated by bare nodes of Ranvier.
options: Correct. A Schwann cell or oligodendrocyte spirals its own membrane around the axon.
Correct. About 70 to 80% of myelin's dry weight is lipid.
Correct. The gaps between myelin segments are nodes of Ranvier.
Incorrect. Myelin is made by glial cells, not by the neuron.
Incorrect. Myelin wraps axons, not the short dendrites of a neuron.

why.correct: Tumors grow from cells that divide. Glial cells keep dividing throughout life, while mature neurons do not, so most brain tumors are gliomas.
options: Correct. A cell that divides can divide out of control; a cell that does not divide cannot form a tumor.
Blood exposure does not explain which cells form tumors. The ability to divide does.
Myelin wraps axons, not whole neurons, and it has nothing to do with tumor formation.
Direct counts find glia and neurons in roughly equal numbers overall. Even if glia were more numerous, cell division, not cell number, is what allows tumors.

why.correct: Ependymal cells line the cavities inside the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord; their cilia help move the fluid, and some help produce it.
options: That is the job of oligodendrocytes.
That is the job of satellite cells in the PNS.
Correct. Ependymal cells form the lining of the CNS's fluid-filled spaces.
That is the job of microglia.

why.correct: A Schwann cell serves a single segment of a single axon and keeps its nucleus and cytoplasm in a living outer layer, the neurilemma. After injury it can clear debris, multiply and form the regeneration tube. An oligodendrocyte serves many axons and forms no such tube.
options: Correct. One axon per cell and a living outer layer let Schwann cells rebuild the path.
Myelin thickness does not decide whether an axon regrows.
Glial cells do not guide regrowth with neurotransmitter. Schwann cells release growth-promoting proteins and provide an adhesive tube.
Schwann cells do not become neurons. The neuron survives and regrows its own axon.

why.correct: Counting dissolved nuclei from whole brains gives about 86 billion neurons and a similar number of other cells, mostly glia: close to one to one overall, with large differences between regions. Some exams still expect the older "ten to one" figure.
options: This is the older textbook figure, and direct counts do not support it overall or in every region.
Neurons do outnumber glia in a few densely packed regions, but not overall.
Correct. The overall ratio is near one to one.
Glial cells make up about half of the brain's cells in adults.

why.correct: Oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells both make myelin; astrocytes and satellite cells both surround neurons and control their surroundings. Ependymal cells have no PNS counterpart.
options: Correct. Each is the myelin maker on its side of the CNS–PNS border.
Correct. Satellite cells do for ganglion neurons much of what astrocytes do in the CNS.
Incorrect. Satellite cells are not the PNS's phagocytes; in a damaged nerve, Schwann cells and macrophages from the blood clear the debris.
Incorrect. Schwann cells wrap axons. Ependymal cells have no PNS equivalent.

why.correct: Sodium can pass only while both gates are open. Depolarization swings the fast activation gate open, and the slower inactivation gate has not yet swung in, so sodium rushes in and drives the rising phase.
options: This is the closed, ready state at rest. The channel can open, but no sodium flows yet.
Correct. For well under a millisecond both gates are open, and sodium floods in.
This is the inactivated state, reached about a millisecond later, at the peak and during the falling phase. No sodium flows.
Both gates are shut only briefly, while a channel resets after repolarization. During the rising phase the activation gate is open.

why.correct: At 1.5 ms the membrane is at the peak, inside the absolute refractory period. Every sodium channel is open or inactivated, so there are no ready channels for a second stimulus to open, however strong it is.
options: Correct. In the absolute refractory period no stimulus can start another action potential.
A smaller second action potential is possible only in the relative refractory period, which begins later, at about 2.1 ms.
Action potentials are all-or-none. A stronger stimulus never makes a taller one, and in this window it cannot make one at all.
The peak is capped by sodium inactivation and potassium opening. Extra stimulus cannot push it higher.

why.correct: At 3 ms the membrane is in the relative refractory period. Only some sodium channels have reset to the ready state, and the slow potassium channels are still open, holding the membrane near −80 mV, farther from threshold. A normal stimulus falls short; a stronger one would work.
options: One action potential moves only a tiny fraction of the ions. The concentrations have barely changed, so the pump is not what limits a second spike.
The potassium channels are still open at 3 ms; that is what holds the membrane below rest. And potassium channels closing would not block a new spike.
Correct. Fewer ready sodium channels plus a membrane pulled below rest mean a normal stimulus cannot reach threshold.
If every sodium channel were inactivated, no stimulus of any strength would work. That describes the absolute refractory period, which ended at about 2.1 ms.

why.correct: The delayed potassium channels close slowly, so for a few milliseconds after repolarization potassium keeps leaving. The membrane drifts toward potassium's equilibrium potential of about −90 mV and dips to about −80 mV before the channels close.
options: The pump works steadily in the background and contributes only a few millivolts. It does not make the dip after each spike.
Chloride channels are not part of the axon's action potential. The dip is carried by potassium.
Open sodium channels would push the membrane up toward +60 mV, not down below rest. At this point they are resetting from the inactivated state.
Correct. Potassium keeps flowing out through slow-closing channels, so the membrane overshoots below rest.

why.correct: A local anesthetic removes ready sodium channels. The resting potential is untouched, but threshold rises, each spike rises more slowly and sends less current forward, conduction slows, and in the most affected fibers action potentials fail altogether.

variables.name: Resting membrane potential
variables.why: Voltage-gated sodium channels are closed at rest. Potassium leak channels and the pump set the resting potential, and the drug does not touch them.

variables.name: Sodium channels available to open
variables.why: The drug blocks half of them, so fewer can open when the membrane depolarizes.

variables.name: Depolarization needed to reach threshold
variables.why: With fewer channels, the membrane must depolarize further before sodium flowing in outruns potassium flowing out.

variables.name: Speed of the rising phase
variables.why: Less sodium enters per moment, so the membrane climbs toward the peak more slowly.

variables.name: Conduction velocity
variables.why: Each firing patch sends less current ahead, so the next patch takes longer to reach threshold.

variables.name: Signals reaching the brain from the numbed area
variables.why: Where too few channels remain, action potentials fail to reach threshold and stop, so fewer signals get through.

why.correct: Myelin does not make action potentials bigger; it keeps current inside the axon so the next node reaches threshold quickly. Strip it away and current leaks out, the next node depolarizes slowly or not at all, and conduction slows or is blocked, while any spike that does fire is still full-sized.

variables.name: Current leaking out across the bare stretch
variables.why: Without the insulating layers of membrane, current escapes through the axon membrane instead of flowing along the inside.

variables.name: Current reaching the next healthy node
variables.why: More leaks out on the way, so less arrives to depolarize the next node.

variables.name: Time for the next node to reach threshold
variables.why: A smaller current depolarizes the node more slowly, so it reaches threshold later, if at all.

variables.name: Conduction velocity through the damaged stretch
variables.why: Each delay at a node adds up, and the bare stretch has few sodium channels to help, so the signal slows or stops.

variables.name: Peak voltage of an action potential at a healthy node that does fire
variables.why: Action potentials are all-or-none. A node that reaches threshold fires a full-sized spike, set by its own channels and gradients.

why.correct: Early on, a smaller potassium gradient moves the resting potential closer to threshold and cells fire more easily. Held depolarized for hours, sodium channels pile up in the inactivated state, threshold rises and spikes shrink or fail. That is why severe hyperkalemia causes weakness and a dangerous heart rhythm rather than nonstop firing.

variables.name: Resting membrane potential (less negative counts as up), early rise
variables.why: More potassium outside shrinks the potassium gradient, so less potassium leaks out and the inside becomes less negative.

variables.name: Ease of reaching threshold, early rise
variables.why: The resting potential now sits a few millivolts closer to −55 mV, and most sodium channels are still ready, so a smaller stimulus reaches threshold.

variables.name: Sodium channels in the closed, ready state, after hours at 8.5 mmol/L
variables.why: A membrane held depolarized for hours lets more and more sodium channels drift into the inactivated state, and they cannot reset without repolarization.

variables.name: Ease of reaching threshold after hours, compared with the early rise
variables.why: With fewer ready sodium channels, threshold rises, so the cells that first fired more easily now fire less easily or not at all.

variables.name: Peak of the action potentials that do fire, after hours
variables.why: Fewer ready sodium channels let in less sodium, and the depolarized starting point shrinks the swing, so the spikes are smaller.

why.correct: Threshold starts the positive feedback of sodium entry, which carries the membrane to the peak. Inactivation stops the sodium inflow as potassium channels open; potassium leaving repolarizes the membrane and, because those channels close slowly, overshoots into the afterhyperpolarization before rest returns.

At the peak the sodium channels inactivate; they do not reset. The inactivation gate plugs the pore, and the channel returns to the ready state only after the membrane repolarizes. That is why the peak is followed by the absolute refractory period.
options: This step is right. At threshold, enough activation gates open that sodium entry outruns potassium exit.
This step is right. Sodium entry drives the rising phase to about +30 mV.
This is the error. At the peak the channels are inactivated, not reset. Resetting needs repolarization and takes a few milliseconds.
This step is right. The delayed potassium channels are open by the peak and carry the falling phase.
This step is right. Slow-closing potassium channels cause the afterhyperpolarization.

why.correct: With sodium inflow stopped, potassium leaving through the now-open delayed potassium channels carries the membrane back down. Those channels are slow to close, which produces the dip below rest that follows.
options: The pump is far too slow to repolarize a membrane in a millisecond. It restores gradients over many action potentials, in the background.
Correct. Potassium outflow is the falling phase, and its slow shutoff causes the dip.
Ligand-gated channels open in response to chemical messengers, not as a step in the axon's action potential.
Without potassium moving out, closing sodium gates alone would leave the membrane depolarized. The falling phase needs potassium outflow.

why.correct: Warmth makes sodium channels inactivate sooner, so each action potential carries a little less current. Healthy axons have plenty to spare. In a demyelinated stretch that was barely bringing the next node to threshold, that small loss causes conduction block. Cooling restores the margin.
options: Myelin is not melted by a shower, and it could not regrow in minutes. The change is too fast to be structural.
Correct. A small, reversible loss of current tips barely-conducting demyelinated axons into block.
Warmth speeds conduction in healthy axons. Only axons already near failure are affected.
Nonstop firing would cause positive symptoms such as flashing lights, not blurring. The resting potential does not rise to threshold in a warm shower.

why.correct: Width and myelin both raise conduction velocity, but myelin has the bigger effect. A myelinated axon 10 µm wide conducts at roughly 50 to 60 m/s; an unmyelinated axon has to be enormously wider to come close.
options: A thin unmyelinated axon conducts at only about 1 m/s: every patch must fire in turn, and its narrow core resists current.
Twice the width of the myelinated axon helps, but without myelin every patch must still fire in turn, which keeps it far slower.
This is the slowest of the four: the thinnest core and no myelin.
Correct. Saltatory conduction in a moderately wide axon beats continuous conduction in a wider one.

why.correct: Time = distance ÷ velocity = 0.9 m ÷ 60 m/s = 0.015 s = 15 ms.
options: This is ten times too short: 0.015 s is 15 ms, not 1.5 ms. Check the conversion from seconds to milliseconds.
This multiplies distance by velocity (0.9 × 60 = 54). Time is distance divided by velocity.
Correct. 0.9 ÷ 60 = 0.015 s, which is 15 ms.
This is ten times too long. 0.015 s × 1,000 = 15 ms.

why.correct: The shortest possible gap between spikes is one absolute refractory period, 1.25 ms = 0.00125 s. 1 s ÷ 0.00125 s = 800 per second. Real neurons fire below this ceiling.
options: This is ten times too low. Recheck the conversion: 1.25 ms is 0.00125 s.
This uses the digits of 1.25 rather than dividing one second by the refractory period.
This is ten times too high. 1 ÷ 0.00125 = 800.
Correct. One second holds 800 gaps of 1.25 ms.

why.correct: A wider core lowers internal resistance, myelin keeps current inside and limits firing to the nodes, and warmth speeds channel opening. Losing myelin, cooling and blocking sodium channels all slow conduction.
options: Demyelination lets current leak out between nodes, so it slows conduction or blocks it.
Correct. Less internal resistance lets current spread farther ahead.
Cold slows channel gating, so conduction slows. That is part of why ice numbs.
Correct. Myelin allows saltatory conduction.
Correct. Channels gate faster at normal body temperature than in a cooled limb.
Fewer sodium channels send less current ahead, so the next patch reaches threshold later.

why.correct: Myelin insulates the internode and very few sodium channels sit there. Current from the firing node flows through the inside of the axon to the next node with little loss, and only the node regenerates the action potential.
options: Correct. Current travels the whole way; only the slow firing step is skipped.
Nothing leaps outside. "Saltatory" describes how the spike seems to hop from node to node; the current runs inside the axon.
The internode has too few sodium channels to fire, and it is not in contact with the extracellular fluid. Firing happens only at the nodes.
A node fires only when current from the previous node depolarizes it to threshold. Without current flowing under the myelin, nothing would reach it.

why.correct: In the relative refractory period some sodium channels have reset, so a strong enough stimulus reaches threshold. Because not all have reset, and potassium channels are still open, the spike is a little smaller than a normal one.
options: That describes the absolute refractory period. In the relative period a stronger-than-normal stimulus can succeed.
A stronger stimulus does not make a taller spike. The peak depends on the channels and gradients, and here fewer channels are ready.
Correct. Fewer ready sodium channels give a slightly smaller spike.
Sodium channels inactivate within about a millisecond whatever the stimulus, so the membrane cannot stay at the peak.

why.correct: The resting potential depends on potassium leak channels and the gradients, not on voltage-gated sodium channels, which are closed at rest. With those channels blocked, depolarization cannot trigger the sodium inflow of an action potential, so nerves to his muscles, including those for breathing, stop conducting.
options: Blocking the leak channels would change the resting potential, which is nearly normal. Tetrodotoxin acts on voltage-gated sodium channels.
A slowly failing pump would not cause weakness within an hour, and the question states the toxin blocks sodium channels.
Correct. The channels the toxin blocks do nothing at rest, but every action potential needs them.
The toxin blocks the channel pore; it does not hold channels open. Channels held open would depolarize the resting membrane.

why.correct: Two things end the rise at once: the inactivation gates plug the sodium channels, stopping the inward flow, and the delayed potassium channels open, starting an outward flow. The membrane turns around before it can reach +60 mV.
options: Only a tiny fraction of the sodium crosses in one action potential. The gradient is almost unchanged.
The pump runs all the time and is far too slow to stop a spike in a fraction of a millisecond.
Because concentrations barely change, sodium's equilibrium potential stays near +60 mV.
Correct. Timing, not the gradient, sets the peak: inactivation plus potassium outflow.

why.correct: In a myelinated axon, current flows under the myelin and the action potential is regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier, so it seems to leap from node to node (Latin saltare, to leap).
options: That is continuous conduction, in an unmyelinated axon.
Correct. Firing only at the nodes is what makes it fast and cheap.
Graded potentials spread passively and fade; they are not conducted this way.
The name comes from the Latin for "to leap", not from salt.

why.correct: An action potential is regenerated at full size by every patch or node it reaches, so it arrives as large as it started. A graded potential fades within a millimeter or two.
options: Correct. Arriving undiminished is the mark of a regenerated, all-or-none signal.
Graded potentials can depolarize too, so a depolarization alone does not tell them apart.
Growing with stimulus strength is the mark of a graded potential. Action potentials stay the same size.
Shrinking with distance is how a graded potential behaves.

why.correct: Synaptic vesicles are the small membrane sacs in the axon terminal that hold neurotransmitter. Calcium entry makes them fuse with the terminal membrane and release it.
options: Correct. These sacs store neurotransmitter until calcium triggers their release.
Mitochondria supply ATP in the terminal, but they are larger, with folded inner membranes, and they do not release neurotransmitter.
Ligand-gated channels sit in the postsynaptic membrane across the cleft, not inside the axon terminal.
Nodes of Ranvier are gaps in the myelin along an axon, not structures inside the axon terminal.

why.correct: The synaptic cleft is the gap, about 20 nm wide, between the axon terminal and the postsynaptic membrane. Neurotransmitter diffuses across it.
options: A synaptic vesicle is a sac inside the axon terminal, not the gap between the two cells.
Correct. This is the gap the neurotransmitter crosses.
A gap junction joins two cells' cytosols directly, at an electrical synapse. Here the cells are separated by a gap, the mark of a chemical synapse.
The axon hillock is where the axon leaves the cell body of a neuron, not the gap at a synapse.

why.correct: Depolarization of the terminal opens calcium channels; calcium triggers exocytosis; the neurotransmitter crosses the cleft and binds receptor proteins; channels open or close, and the ion flow produces an EPSP or IPSP in the postsynaptic cell. Removal of the neurotransmitter then ends the signal.
Calcium flows into the terminal down a steep electrochemical gradient and binds sensor proteins on the docked vesicles, which triggers them to fuse and release their contents.
options: Sodium enters the axon during the action potential, not the cleft, and it is not the trigger for release.
Correct. Calcium entry is the link between the electrical signal and release.
Acetylcholinesterase acts in the cleft on released acetylcholine. It does not act on vesicles.
The postsynaptic neuron can respond only after neurotransmitter has been released and bound, which comes later.

why.correct: Calcium, not sodium, triggers release. Depolarization of the terminal opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and calcium entering binds sensor proteins on the vesicles.
options: This step is right. The arriving action potential depolarizes the terminal membrane.
This is the error. The trigger for vesicle fusion is calcium entering through voltage-gated calcium channels.
This step is right. The neurotransmitter crosses the 20 nm cleft by diffusion.
This step is right. Binding to receptor proteins opens or closes ion channels.
This step is right. Reuptake is one of the ways the signal ends.

why.correct: Near-instant, two-way transfer of current is the signature of an electrical synapse: gap junctions let ions flow straight from one cytosol into the other.
options: Even a fast chemical synapse has a synaptic delay of about half a millisecond, and it works only from presynaptic to postsynaptic.
Metabotropic effects take tens of milliseconds or more, and they are one-way.
Correct. Ions pass directly through gap junctions, in either direction.
A neuromuscular junction links a neuron to a skeletal muscle fiber, not two neurons, and it is a one-way chemical synapse.

why.correct: The action potential depends on sodium and potassium, so it still travels to the terminal and opens the calcium channels. With no calcium outside, nothing flows in, the vesicles are not triggered, and release fails.
options: Conduction along the axon uses sodium and potassium channels, not calcium, so the action potential still arrives.
Without release there are no EPSPs from this input, so the postsynaptic neuron is less likely to fire, not more.
Correct. Calcium entry is the trigger for exocytosis.
Diffusion does not need calcium. The problem comes earlier: without calcium, there is almost nothing released to diffuse.

why.correct: Blocking reuptake removes the main exit route for serotonin. Each release lasts longer and activates postsynaptic receptor proteins more, while the steps that cause release are unchanged.

variables.name: Serotonin taken back into the presynaptic terminal
variables.why: The transporters that perform reuptake are blocked.

variables.name: Time serotonin stays in the synaptic cleft after each release
variables.why: With reuptake, the main removal route, blocked, only slow diffusion clears serotonin from the cleft.

variables.name: Activation of postsynaptic serotonin receptor proteins
variables.why: Serotonin that lingers binds the receptor proteins again and again, so they are active for longer.

variables.name: Calcium entry into the terminal per action potential
variables.why: The drug acts on the reuptake transporters, not on the voltage-gated calcium channels that open when the action potential arrives.

why.correct: The nerve releases the usual amount of acetylcholine, but nothing clears it quickly. It keeps binding nicotinic receptor proteins, so each impulse causes a long depolarization: at first twitching, and with a large dose, weakness as the muscle fibers stay depolarized.

variables.name: Acetylcholinesterase activity in the synaptic cleft
variables.why: The poison binds the enzyme and stops it working.

variables.name: Time acetylcholine stays in the cleft after each nerve impulse
variables.why: Acetylcholine is no longer split in about a millisecond, so it lingers until it slowly diffuses away.

variables.name: Acetylcholine released per nerve action potential
variables.why: Release depends on calcium entering the terminal, which the poison does not change.

variables.name: Duration of the end plate depolarization after each impulse
variables.why: Lingering acetylcholine keeps opening nicotinic receptor proteins, so the depolarization lasts longer.

why.correct: Point A sits above rest but below the −55 mV line. The EPSPs have summed, but not by enough to reach threshold, so no action potential fires.
options: The refractory period follows an action potential, and none has fired yet.
Correct. Summation has moved the membrane toward threshold but not to it.
The stepwise climb to A shows the EPSPs adding; that is summation.
The trigger zone, the initial segment just beyond the hillock, has the densest voltage-gated sodium channels in the neuron. The problem at A is simply that the sum is below threshold.

why.correct: The magenta segments are IPSPs. Inhibitory synapses open chloride or potassium channels, which pull the membrane away from threshold and subtract from the EPSPs that came before.
options: No action potential has fired at A. The trace fell from below threshold, so this is not a falling phase.
Reuptake ends a neurotransmitter's action; it does not drive the membrane downward by itself.
Correct. IPSPs subtract from the summed EPSPs.
An afterhyperpolarization follows an action potential, and there has been none before A.

why.correct: Panel B shows temporal summation. E1 fires every 3 ms, and an EPSP takes longer than that to fade, so each new one starts from a higher base and the sum climbs to threshold.
options: Correct. Repeated input from one source adds up over time.
The threshold line stays at −55 mV in every panel.
That would be spatial summation, shown in panel C. Panel B is one input firing repeatedly.
The three EPSPs in panel B are the same size; they reach threshold by stacking, not by growing.

why.correct: EPSPs and IPSPs add algebraically. Removing the IPSP and adding more simultaneous EPSPs, as in panel C, gives enough depolarization to reach threshold.
options: More IPSPs subtract more from the EPSP and push the membrane further from threshold.
Blocking reuptake of an inhibitory neurotransmitter prolongs its effect, making the IPSP larger and longer.
Correct. More excitation and no inhibition is what panel C shows reaching threshold.
Less calcium outside means less neurotransmitter released from the excitatory terminal, so a smaller EPSP.

why.correct: With chloride channels open, any depolarization away from −70 mV makes chloride flow in, which pulls the membrane back toward −70 mV. The excitatory inputs produce smaller depolarizations, so the neuron is less likely to reach threshold. Inhibition does not always need a visible hyperpolarization.
options: The effect shows up only when other inputs try to move the membrane: open chloride channels hold it near −70 mV.
Chloride entering carries negative charge in during any depolarization, which works against the excitatory inputs.
GABA's chloride channels hold the membrane near rest, which keeps voltage-gated sodium channels closed.
Correct. Clamping the membrane near rest is still inhibition.

why.correct: The receptor protein decides the effect. Skeletal muscle has ionotropic nicotinic receptor proteins, which let sodium in and depolarize the fiber. The heart cells that set its rate have metabotropic receptor proteins, which through a G protein open potassium channels and slow them.
options: Acetylcholine is the same molecule wherever it is released.
Correct. Same neurotransmitter, different receptor proteins, different results.
Faster breakdown would shorten an effect, not reverse it.
Heart cells rely on voltage-gated channels for their action potentials.

why.correct: Slow onset, long duration and dependence on G proteins are the marks of a metabotropic receptor protein, which works through a G protein and often a second messenger.
options: Correct. G protein signaling explains the delay, the long duration and the drug's effect.
Ionotropic receptor proteins are channels that open within a millisecond and close within milliseconds; they do not need G proteins.
Voltage-gated channels respond to membrane potential, not to a neurotransmitter binding.
Gap junctions pass current directly between cells; no neurotransmitter is involved.

why.correct: Metabotropic receptor proteins are G-protein-coupled receptor proteins. They work more slowly and for longer than channels, amplify signals through second messengers, and can change enzymes and gene expression.
options: Correct. The G protein is the link to everything they do.
They have no pore. An instant-opening pore describes an ionotropic receptor protein.
Correct. G protein and second messenger effects outlast the neurotransmitter's binding.
Correct. One bound receptor protein can lead to many second messenger molecules.
Nicotinic receptor proteins at the neuromuscular junction are ionotropic: they are ligand-gated channels.
Correct. Second messengers can switch on enzymes that change gene expression.

why.correct: The membrane needs 15 mV of depolarization. 7 × 3 − 4 = 17 mV, which takes it to −53 mV, past threshold. Each of the other sets falls short.
options: 4 × 3 = 12 mV, reaching −58 mV: below threshold.
6 × 3 − 4 = 14 mV, reaching −56 mV: just short of threshold.
5 × 3 − 2 × 4 = 7 mV, reaching −63 mV: well below threshold.
Correct. 21 − 4 = 17 mV, reaching −53 mV.

why.correct: Action potentials still reach the terminal and calcium still enters, but the vesicles cannot fuse, so acetylcholine is not released. Muscle fibers get no signal, and they are weak and floppy.
options: The toxin acts at the terminal, after conduction. The action potential still arrives.
Receptor proteins are unaffected; there is simply no acetylcholine to bind them.
Blocking breakdown would leave extra acetylcholine and cause twitching, the opposite of floppy weakness.
Correct. No vesicle fusion means no release.

why.correct: Fentanyl slows breathing by activating the metabotropic receptor proteins that endorphins normally use. Naloxone binds the same receptor proteins but does not switch them on. Given in a large enough dose, it crowds fentanyl off them and removes its effect.
options: Correct. Naloxone competes for the same receptor proteins and leaves them inactive.
Naloxone is not an enzyme. It acts at the receptor proteins, and fentanyl is cleared later by the liver.
Endorphins act on the same receptor proteins as fentanyl, so prolonging them would add to the problem.
Opening chloride channels would add inhibition and slow breathing further.

why.correct: A motor neuron's firing depends on the sum of its EPSPs and IPSPs. With the inhibitory interneurons silenced, the IPSPs disappear, the same excitatory inputs now push the motor neurons past threshold again and again, and their muscles contract hard and uncontrollably.
options: The toxin acts on inhibitory interneurons in the CNS, not on muscle fibers.
Correct. Removing inhibition leaves excitation unopposed.
Failed acetylcholine release would cause floppy weakness, as in botulism, not spasms.
The toxin blocks release from inhibitory interneurons; it does not act on the enzyme at the neuromuscular junction.

why.correct: Glutamate drives most fast excitatory synapses in the brain and spinal cord, mainly through ionotropic receptor proteins that let sodium in. GABA and glycine are the main inhibitory ones.
options: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain.
Acetylcholine excites skeletal muscle and acts in the brain, but most fast excitatory synapses in the CNS use glutamate.
Correct. Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter of the CNS.
Serotonin is a biogenic amine that mostly adjusts neuron activity through metabotropic receptor proteins; it is not the main fast excitatory neurotransmitter.

why.correct: Biogenic amines are made from single amino acids: dopamine and norepinephrine from tyrosine, serotonin from tryptophan. Glutamate and GABA are amino acid neurotransmitters, and endorphins are neuropeptides.
options: Glutamate is an amino acid neurotransmitter, not an amine made from one.
Correct. Dopamine is a biogenic amine.
Endorphins are neuropeptides: short chains of amino acids.
Correct. Serotonin is a biogenic amine.
Correct. Norepinephrine is a biogenic amine.
GABA is grouped with the amino acid neurotransmitters.

why.correct: One presynaptic neuron reaching many postsynaptic neurons is divergence: one signal spreads to many cells.
options: Correct. One to many is divergence.
Convergence is the reverse: many presynaptic neurons synapsing on one.
Spatial summation happens within one postsynaptic neuron when several inputs arrive together; it is not a wiring pattern.
Nothing here says the synapses use gap junctions; this is a question about wiring, not synapse type.
